The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon\nu(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1	o S^3$ be a smooth oriented embedding and write its quotient normal bundle as $
u_K=K^*TS^3/dK(TS^1)$. Choose an orientation-preserving trivialization $
u_K\cong S^1	imes\mathbb R^2$ and a tubular map $\Phi:\Omega	o S^3$, meaning a smooth embedding from an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq
u_K$ of the zero section onto an open neighbourhood of $K(S^1)$ with $\Phi(s,0)=K(s)$, such that in these product coordinates $\Omega$ contains $S^1	imes D^2_{2\epsilon}$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Here $D^2_r=\{z\in\mathbb R^2:\|z\|\le r\}$. Set $N(K)=\Phi(S^1	imes D^2_\epsilon)$, $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$, $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ be inclusion, $p:T_K	o S^1$ the product projection, and $\mu$ the positive boundary of a normal disk, using the normal-plane orientation determined by the orientations of $K$ and $S^3$. A class is primitive if it is not $m$ times another class for any integer $|m|>1$. Then $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is generated by $[\mu]$. The kernel of $i_*:H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)	o H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is a primitive rank-one direct summand generated by a unique class $[\lambda]$ with $p_*[\lambda]=1\in H_1(S^1;\mathbb Z)$. It has a simple closed representative, is the preferred longitude, and $([\mu],[\lambda])$ is a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

Let $T=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z^2$ be oriented by $dx\wedge dy$, and identify $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^2$ in the standard basis, so the algebraic intersection of classes $v,w$ is $\det(v,w)$. Let $\gamma_0,\gamma_1\subset T$ be smooth embedded circles that are not null-homotopic. Orient them so that their homology classes agree, and suppose their common class $v\in H_1(T;\mathbb Z)$ is primitive, meaning it is not an integer multiple $m u$ with $|m|>1$. Then $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ are isotopic through embedded circles in $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, its Seifert genus is zero if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth three-manifold, possibly nonorientable and with boundary, and let $f:F\to M$ be a smooth embedding of a compact smooth surface with $f^{-1}(\partial M)=\partial F$. Transversality to $\partial M$ is not assumed. Given an open neighborhood $U$ of $C=f(\partial F)$, there is a jointly smooth map $(x,t)\mapsto f_t(x)$ such that each $f_t$ is an embedding, $f_0=f$, every $f_t$ agrees with $f$ on $\partial F$ and outside $f^{-1}(U)$, and $f_t$ is neatly proper for every $t>0$. Time may instead be reparametrized to be stationary near both endpoints; in that version neatness holds after the initial stationary interval.

There is also a jointly continuous ambient isotopy of homeomorphisms $H_t:M\to M$, starting at the identity, supported in $U$, fixing $\partial M$ pointwise, and satisfying $H_t f=f_t$. The construction makes $H_t$ jointly smooth on $(M\setminus C)\times[0,1]$. If $f$ is already neat, the same $f_t$ alternatively admits a jointly smooth ambient extension fixing $\partial M$. No smooth ambient extension at an original tangency is asserted.

derivations.claim: Under the full-AC hypothesis [F1], the supplier in [F2] applies. Since $c$ is essential on the torus, it is nonseparating: a separating simple curve on a genus-one surface cuts off a disk on one side and is null-homotopic. Cutting the torus along $c$ therefore gives a connected orientable surface with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero, hence an annulus. An embedded arc joining its two boundary circles closes after regluing to a loop meeting $c$ transversely once. The algebraic intersection is therefore $\pm1$, so $[c]$ is primitive in $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$.

Because $c=\partial D$, its image in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$ is zero. By [F2], write $[c]=q[\lambda]$ for an integer $q$. Since both $[c]$ and $[\lambda]$ are primitive, $q=\pm1$. Orient $c$ to make $[c]=[\lambda]$. By [F3], $c$ is isotopic on $T_K$ to a chosen simple representative of the preferred longitude.

In product coordinates $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, the curve $c$ has core degree one by [F2], so its torus class is $(1,k)$ for an integer $k$. The graph $\gamma_k(t)=(e^{it},e^{ikt})$ has that class. By [F3], choose a smooth isotopy $c_s(t)=(u_s(t),z_s(t))$ on the boundary torus from $c$ to $\gamma_k$, stationary near its final time after smooth reparametrization. This isotopy need not trace an embedded annulus on the torus itself. Instead choose a smooth strictly decreasing radius $r(s)$ from $1$ to $1/2$ with nonzero derivative, and use $(s,t)\mapsto(u_s(t),r(s)z_s(t))$ in the tube. Distinct $s$ have distinct radii, while each fixed-$s$ curve is embedded; moreover the time derivative has nonzero radial component and is independent of its circle tangent. This gives a smooth embedded annulus with outer boundary exactly $c$ and inner boundary the radius-$1/2$ copy of $\gamma_k$. Continue it inward by $(r,t)\mapsto(e^{it},r e^{ikt})$ for $0\le r\le1/2$. The stationary final curve makes the collars agree; the inward annulus is smooth and regular even at $r=0$ and has core boundary $K$. The resulting annulus lies otherwise in the interior of $N(K)$.

If the given disk is only boundary-preimage embedded, first replace it using [F5] by a neat smooth disk in $E_K$ with the same boundary $c$. The annulus of step 3.1 has nonzero inward radial derivative at $c$ on the tube side. The resulting proper disk $D$ on the exterior side and this annulus on the tube side meet only along $c$. Their union is an embedded disk with boundary $K$; smoothing the corner along $c$ in a product collar leaves that boundary fixed. Thus $K$ bounds a smooth disk, which is a genus-zero Seifert surface. Full AC supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F4], so [F4] makes $K$ ambient isotopic to the unknot, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore no such disk $D$ exists.

Let $D$ be a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram in an oriented $3$-sphere, with finite crossing set $C(D)$. Fix a unit viewing normal $n$ and orient the projection plane $P$ so $(u,v)$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is positive in the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, define its sign as the sign of $\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$, where the two nonzero projected tangent vectors follow the oriented over- and under-strands. Let $n_+$ and $n_-$ be the numbers of positive and negative crossings.

Set $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, with $\deg(1)=1$ and $\deg(X)=-1$. Its unit, multiplication, counit, and comultiplication are
$$
\eta(1)=1,\qquad m(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m(1\otimes X)=m(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m(X\otimes X)=0,
$$
$$
\epsilon(1)=0,\quad\epsilon(X)=1,\qquad \Delta(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad\Delta(X)=X\otimes X.
$$
Thus $m$ and $\Delta$ have quantum degree $-1$, while $\eta$ and $\epsilon$ have degree $+1$.

Choose a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on $C(D)$. A resolution state is a function $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$; at $v(c)=0$ use the A-smoothing and at $v(c)=1$ use the B-smoothing from the Kauffman source chart. Write $|v|=\sum_c v(c)$, let $D_v$ be the crossingless resolution, and let $k(v)$ be its number of circles. Assign the state module $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$. For an edge $v\to v+e_j$ changing crossing $c_j$ from $0$ to $1$, use $m$ if the local smoothing merges two circles and $\Delta$ if it splits one circle, tensored with the identity on all other factors, and multiply this map by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. The resulting direct sum has cohomological degree
$$i(v)=|v|-n_-$$
and the generator with circle labels $1$ or $X$ has quantum degree
$$j(v)=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{\text{circle labels }a}\deg(a).$$
This defines the normalized integral Khovanov cube and its candidate degree-zero cochain differential; the assertion that the differential squares to zero is a separate lemma.

The Frobenius identity that controls a merge-split face is represented by the two equal composites below. The diagram records the maps only; the proof verifies the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$ and does not rely on the drawing.

```tikzcd
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"m"] \arrow[d,"\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathcal A \arrow[d,"\Delta"] \\
\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m"'] & \mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A
```

**Input:** a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ and a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on its crossing set. A diagram object is supplied as mathematical input; this procedure does not parse a serialized string.

**Output:** the normalized bigraded Khovanov cochain module $C^{i,j}(D)$ and its candidate differential $d:C^{i,j}(D)\to C^{i+1,j}(D)$, constructed by the following finite instructions.

1. Enumerate every state $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$ once. Form the crossingless resolution by using the A-smoothing at $v(c)=0$ and the B-smoothing at $v(c)=1$.
2. For each state, create one tensor factor of the integral Frobenius algebra for each resolution circle and place the resulting tensor product in cohomological degree $|v|-n_-$ and quantum degree $|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$ for its circle labels $a$.
3. For each state and each crossing $c_j$ with $v(c_j)=0$, create the edge to $v+e_j$. Apply multiplication if that smoothing change merges two circles, comultiplication if it splits one circle, the identity on other tensor factors, and the sign $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. Sum the edge maps out of every state to obtain $d$.
4. Return the finite direct sum of the state modules with these degrees and maps. The square-zero property is the separate local lemma named by `justified_by`.

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Edges not meeting the interval use $m$ or $\Delta$. This based tangle cube is the quotient complex above, with the stated quantum shift.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram, order its crossings as $c_1<\cdots<c_n$, and form the direct sum of state modules $\mathcal A^{\otimes k(v)}$ over all functions $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$. Here $\mathcal A=\mathbb Z[X]/(X^2)$, each crossing is changed from its A-smoothing at $0$ to its B-smoothing at $1$, and the edge map is the multiplication $m$ for a merge or comultiplication $\Delta$ for a split, multiplied by $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$ on the edge at $c_j$. Then the sum $d$ of all edge maps satisfies $d^2=0$.

derivations.claim: The crossingless diagram has one based circle, hence its reduced state module is $M=\mathbb Z\{1\}$ in degree $0$ by [F2]–[F3]. There are no crossings and therefore no differential, so its cohomology is $\mathbb Z$ in degree $0$.

First compute the auxiliary positive two-strand closure, whose $A$-smoothing is the identity tangle and whose $B$-smoothing is the cap-cup tangle. This is only an auxiliary raw cube; it does not change the specified negative diagram. With zero, one, two, or three cap-cup smoothings, the closure has respectively two, one, two, or three circles: composing cap-cups creates one additional internal circle each time after the first. Thus its four raw cochain degrees $0,1,2,3$ have modules $M\otimes\mathcal A$, $M^3$, $(M\otimes\mathcal A)^3$, and $M\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal A$, of ranks $2,3,6,4$.

Order crossings from top to bottom. The first differential sends $1\otimes1$ to $(1,1,1)$ and $1\otimes X$ to zero, so its image is the diagonal copy of $\mathbb Z$ and its kernel is $\mathbb Z\{1\otimes X\}$. After suppressing the common based factor $M$, the next differential is the signed incidence matrix
$$
\begin{pmatrix}-1&1&0\\-1&0&1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}
$$
with each integer entry multiplying the label $X$, because each edge splits the based circle and the reduced split sends $1$ to $1\otimes X$. Its image has rank two and its kernel is the diagonal copy of $\mathbb Z$.

Label the three two-circle states in crossing order and identify the two unbased factors in the all-$B$ state from left to right. The last differential is
$$
(a,b,c)\longmapsto a\otimes X-\Delta(b)+X\otimes c.
$$
Here the first and third edges split the based circle, while the middle edge splits the unbased circle; the signs are the cube signs from [F2]. Its image is exactly the subgroup generated by $1\otimes X$, $X\otimes1$, and $X\otimes X$, and its kernel consists of triples with equal coefficients of $1$ and with coefficients of $X$ satisfying $a_X-b_X+c_X=0$.

These auxiliary raw differentials have ranks $1,2,3$. Their images are primitive subgroups of their target free groups: the first image has a coordinate $1$, the incidence matrix in step 1.3 has a $2$ by $2$ minor $1$, and the last image is the coordinate span of $1\otimes X,X\otimes1,X\otimes X$. In each case elementary integral row and column elimination therefore gives only unit nonzero diagonal entries. Hence all auxiliary homology groups are free. The kernel/image calculations in steps 1.3 and 1.4 give raw cohomology $\mathbb Z$ in degrees $0,2,3$ and zero in degree $1$.

Now return to the specified negative diagram. At each crossing its A-smoothing is cap-cup and its B-smoothing is through, so the state $v$ has exactly the same circles as the auxiliary positive state $w=1-v$. Put the perfect integral pairing $\langle a,b\rangle=\epsilon(ab)$ on each unbased circle, with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, and pair the based module $M$ with itself by $\langle1,1\rangle=1$. Multiplication and comultiplication are adjoints for these pairings, directly on $1,X$; the reduced merge and split are adjoints too, since $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$, $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$ and $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$. Use the same actual circle order on the two complementary states. For an edge in coordinate $j$, the old transposed sign is $(-1)^{j-1-\sum_{k<j}v_k}$ whereas the negative cube requires $(-1)^{\sum_{k<j}v_k}$. Multiplying vertex $v$ by $J(v)=(-1)^{\sum_j(j-1)v_j}$ corrects this ratio: across that edge its ratio is $(-1)^{j-1}$. Thus the negative raw cube is integrally isomorphic to the degree-reversed transpose of the auxiliary cube, with this explicit diagonal sign correction. No spatial reflection or change to the given negative crossing is used.

The reversed transpose has ranks $4,6,3,2$ in raw degrees $0,1,2,3$, and differential ranks $3,2,1$. Transposition preserves the unit diagonal entries proved in step 2.1, as do the unimodular pairings and $J$ in step 2.2. Each image is therefore primitive; its quotient in the kernel is torsion-free because it is a subgroup of the free quotient of the whole target. Rank-nullity now gives free homology of ranks $1,1,0,1$ in raw degrees $0,1,2,3$. The negative diagram has three negative crossings, so the normalization $i=|v|-3$ gives $\mathbb Z$ exactly in degrees $-3,-2,0$, with zero in degree $-1$. Together with step 1.1 this proves all stated ranks for the actual two diagrams.

citations.quote: Fix the orientation-reversing involution $r:S^3\to S^3$ given by reflection across a fixed equatorial two-sphere containing a chosen standard unknot $U$. For a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, its mirror is $\overline K:=r(K)$, with the orientation transported by $r$. A diagram of the mirror can be obtained by keeping the projected shadow fixed and interchanging the over- and under-crossing data at every crossing; equivalently, one may reflect the planar shadow while retaining the crossing data. These are alternative mirror conventions, not operations to perform together. Since $r^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $r(U)=U$, mirroring twice returns $K$, and $K$ is the unknot exactly when $\overline K$ is.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $K$ be an oriented knot and let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular oriented diagrams of $K$ with basepoints away from all crossings. Then the reduced integral groups $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$ and $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D',p')$ are isomorphic for every $(i,\widetilde j)$. In particular, they are invariant under Reidemeister moves supported away from the basepoint and under transport of the basepoint along the knot.

Assume full AC. Let $D$ be a finite based diagram of a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$ with ordered crossings $c_1<\cdots<c_n$. The singular instanton resolution complex admits a finite filtration whose first page, with its first differential, is isomorphic to the reduced Khovanov cube of the reflected based diagram $\overline D$. Its spectral sequence converges to $I^\natural(K;\mathbb Z)$. The cube sign at the edge changing $c_j$ is $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v_i}$, and the edge operation is multiplication for a merge or comultiplication for a split. Thus its $E_2$ page is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology of $\overline D$. citations.quote: Fix the orientation-reversing involution $r:S^3\to S^3$ given by reflection across a fixed equatorial two-sphere containing a chosen standard unknot $U$. For a smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, its mirror is $\overline K:=r(K)$, with the orientation transported by $r$. On a diagram this reflects the projection and interchanges the over- and under-crossing data. Since $r^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $r(U)=U$, mirroring twice returns $K$, and $K$ is the unknot exactly when $\overline K$ is.

Let $(D,p)$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a knot with a basepoint $p$ away from the crossings, and let $C(D)$ be its normalized integral Khovanov cochain complex. At each resolution state, let $X_p$ act by multiplication by $X$ on the tensor factor for the circle containing $p$, and by the identity on every other circle factor. The basepoint action is the direct sum of these statewise maps. Define the reduced cochain complex by
$$\widetilde C(D,p):=C(D)/\operatorname{im}(X_p),$$
with the same cohomological grading and with reduced quantum degree $\widetilde j=j-1$ for the class represented by a state whose basepoint circle is labelled $1$. Its cohomology is the reduced integral Khovanov cohomology $\widetilde{Kh}^{i,\widetilde j}(D,p)$. The unknot is normalized so that its reduced group lies in bidegree $(0,0)$.

Equivalently, cut the based knot at $p$ to a one-interval tangle. Put $M=\mathbb Z$ in quantum degree $0$ with $X\cdot1=0$. A resolution with $k$ closed circles and the distinguished interval is assigned $\mathcal A^{\otimes k}\otimes M$. An edge that merges a circle into the interval uses $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$ and $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$; an edge that splits the interval uses $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$, where the circle factor is written first and the interval factor second. Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a fixed finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let $r>0$, and write $B_r=B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$. For each $f\in L^2(B_r;V)$ with $\int_{B_r}f=0$ there exists a unique $u\in W^{2,2}(B_r;V)$ with $\int_{B_r}u=0$ satisfying the Neumann problem in the weak form
$$\int_{B_r}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{B_r}\langle f,v\rangle\qquad\bigl(v\in W^{1,2}(B_r;V)\bigr).$$
Thus $-\Delta u=f$ distributionally, and the zero-normal boundary condition is included in the displayed all-test-function identity. The inverse $f\mapsto u$ is linear and obeys
$$\|D^2u\|_2\le\|f\|_2,\qquad r^{-2}\|u\|_2+r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2+\|D^2u\|_2\le C\|f\|_2,$$
with $C$ independent of $r$ and $f$. The Hessian norm is the Euclidean norm on all ordered second derivatives. If $f$ is the restriction of a polynomial and has mean zero, then $u$ is the restriction of a polynomial with classical $\partial_\nu u=0$ on $\partial B_r$.

If a fixed finite $\Gamma\le O(4)$ and an orthogonal representation $\sigma:\Gamma\to O(V)$ satisfy $f(\gamma x)=\sigma(\gamma)f(x)$ almost everywhere, the unique solution satisfies $u(\gamma x)=\sigma(\gamma)u(x)$ almost everywhere. This includes $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with its Frobenius norm and a prescribed action by orthogonal Lie-algebra automorphisms.

The compatibility $\int f=0$ is necessary. This is a linear $L^2$ boundary-solvability result; higher-$L^p$ Neumann estimates and nonlinear Coulomb-gauge existence are separate assertions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$ and $1<p<\infty$. Then there is $C=C(n,p)<\infty$ such that every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies
$$\|D^2u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|\Delta u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)},\qquad \|\partial_i\partial_ju\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le C\|\Delta u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)},$$
for all $i,j$, where $\|D^2u\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=2}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$; by density the bound extends to every $u\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ (for which $\Delta u\in L^p$ holds automatically). The constant may be taken as the square of the Riesz-transform bound of [[cor-riesz-transforms-are-bounded-on-lp]], hence is finite throughout $1<p<\infty$, including $p=2$. No sharp endpoint growth rate is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$ and $1<p<\infty$, and for a function with the relevant weak derivatives write $\|Du\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=1}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$ and $\|D^2u\|_{L^p}:=\max_{|\beta|=2}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p}$, equivalent to the sum-form Sobolev norms of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] up to constants depending on $n$. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C=C(n,p,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that every $u\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^n)$ satisfies
$$\|Du\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}\le\varepsilon\|D^2u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}+C\|u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}.$$
The scaled form on balls, with the norm over the doubled ball on the right, is
$$\|Du\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}\le\varepsilon R\|D^2u\|_{L^p(B_{2R}(x_0))}+C R^{-1}\|u\|_{L^p(B_{2R}(x_0))}\qquad\bigl(u\in W^{2,p}(B_{2R}(x_0))\bigr),$$
with $C$ independent of $R$ and $x_0$. This is the absorption inequality used in the frozen-coefficient $W^{2,p}$ estimates. The result is asserted for the strict range $1<p<\infty$ only; the form with the same ball on both sides is not claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.
Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $A\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$ be a unital subalgebra which separates points. Then $A$ is dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$ for the supremum metric.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the intersection
$$C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
is dense in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is a function
$v\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\|v-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ and no
extension of $u$ beyond $\Omega$ is assumed. The exponent $p=\infty$ is
excluded, as the companion remark records.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
[[def-convergence-almost-everywhere-relative-to-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

**Reflection matching.** Let $u$ be smooth near $\overline B_1$ with $\partial_
u u=0$. On $1<|x|<2$ put $\iota(x)=x/|x|^2$ and $v(x)=u(\iota(x))$, and put $v=u$ on $B_1$. At $|x|=1$, $D\iota=I-2
u\otimes
u$; since $
abla u$ is tangential, the outside gradient $D\iota^T
abla u$ equals the inside gradient. The values match as well. Thus $v$ is $C^1$ across the sphere, smooth on each side, and has locally bounded piecewise second derivatives. Integration by parts on the two sides cancels the interface terms for $v$ and its first derivatives, so these piecewise derivatives are its weak derivatives through order two.

**The reflected equation.** Writing $s=|x|$, one has $D\iota=s^{-2}(I-2x\otimes x/s^2)$, $D\iota D\iota^T=s^{-4}I$, and $\Delta\iota_j=-4s^{-4}x_j$ in four dimensions. The chain rule therefore gives $\Delta v=s^{-4}(\Delta u)(\iota x)-4s^{-4}x\cdot(
abla u)(\iota x)$. Since $x\cdot
abla v=-s^{-2}x\cdot(
abla u)(\iota x)$, this is $\Delta v=s^{-4}(\Delta u)(\iota x)+4s^{-2}x\cdot
abla v$. All coefficients are bounded on the annulus. The inversion Jacobian has absolute value $s^{-8}$ and maps that annulus into $B_1\setminus\overline B_{1/2}$, so change of variables bounds its reflected $u$, first-derivative and Laplacian norms by constant multiples of their norms on $B_1$.

**A whole-space estimate for the extension.** Choose the cutoff $\chi$ of [F5] equal to one near $\overline B_1$, and define $Eu=\chi v$ on $B_2$, zero elsewhere. Step 1.1 gives $Eu\in W^{2,p}(\mathbb R^4)$ with compact support. Step 2.1 and $\Delta(\chi v)=\chi\Delta v+2
abla\chi\cdot
abla v+(\Delta\chi)v$ give $\|Eu\|_p\le C\|u\|_p$ and $\|\Delta Eu\|_p\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|
abla u\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. Since $Eu=u$ on $B_1$, $\|
abla u\|_p\le\|
abla Eu\|_p$. Apply [F2] to obtain $\|D^2Eu\|_p\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|
abla Eu\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. Interpolate the middle term by [F2] with $\eta>0$ chosen so $C_p\eta\le1/2$, and absorb it. Then interpolate once more for the first derivatives and restrict to $B_1$. The result is $\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(B_1)}\le C_p(\|\Delta u\|_p+\|u\|_p)$. No estimate was applied before the reflected function's $W^{2,p}$ membership was proved.

**Removing the zeroth-order term for Neumann solutions.** For mean-zero polynomial $f$, [F1] gives a polynomial mean-zero solution $u$ with classical zero normal derivative and $\|u\|_{W^{2,2}}\le C\|f\|_2$. By [F3], $\|u\|_p\le C_p\|f\|_2\le C_p|B_1|^{1/2-1/p}\|f\|_p$, where the final Holder bound uses $p\ge2$. Substitution in step 3.1, with $-\Delta u=f$, proves $\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(B_1)}\le C_{p,V}\|f\|_p$ for these polynomial solutions, uniformly in their degrees.

**Construction for all mean-zero Lp data.** Extend $f$ by zero to $\mathbb R^4$, approximate in $L^p$ by smooth functions using [F4], and restrict to the closed ball. Each approximant is continuous there and hence uniformly approximable by polynomials by [F4]. A choice of uniform error tending to zero gives polynomial approximants in $L^p$; subtract their means to obtain mean-zero $f_j\to f$ in $L^p$, since $\|(f_j-f)_{B_1}\|\,|B_1|^{1/p}\le\|f_j-f\|_p$ before normalization. Let $u_j$ be the polynomial solutions from [F1]. Applying step 4.1 to their differences makes all derivative components through order two Cauchy in $L^p$. Completeness [F4] and passage in the weak-derivative test identities give a limit $u\in W^{2,p}$ with $u_j\to u$ strongly and the same bound. Finite volume and $p\ge2$ imply $u_j\to u$ in $W^{1,2}$ and $f_j\to f$ in $L^2$; their weak Neumann identities pass to the limit for every $W^{1,2}$ test. Thus the solution is the unique $L^2$ Neumann solution of [F1], now with the stronger regularity and norm estimate.

**The complete normalized domain.** By step 5.1 the inverse maps into $X_p^0$ and is bounded there. Conversely let $u\in X_p^0$ and choose polynomial zero-normal approximants $u_j\to u$ in $W^{2,p}$. Subtracting their means preserves the normal condition and convergence. The sources $f_j=-\Delta u_j$ have zero mean, by the polynomial weak identity of [F1], and converge to $f=-\Delta u\in L^p_0$. Each $u_j$ is the normalized solution for $f_j$, so the bounded inverse from step 5.1 sends $f$ to $u$. This proves bijectivity. Also $\|\Delta u\|_p\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,p}}$ and the inverse bound gives the reverse norm comparison. The zero-mean subspace of $L^p$ is closed, since its mean functional is bounded by Holder, hence complete by [F4]. Its isomorphism with $X_p^0$ gives completeness for $\|\Delta u\|_p$.

**Scaling, uniqueness and symmetry.** For $B_r$ put $f_r(y)=r^2f(ry)$, solve on $B_1$ and set $u(x)=u_r(x/r)$. Direct change of variables gives $\|f_r\|_p=r^{2-4/p}\|f\|_p$, $\|D^2u_r\|_p=r^{2-4/p}\|D^2u\|_p$, $\|\nabla u_r\|_p=r^{1-4/p}\|\nabla u\|_p$, and $\|u_r\|_p=r^{-4/p}\|u\|_p$. Assume [[def-countable-choice|Countable Choice]], let $n\ge1$, and let
$1\le j\le n$. On $L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ define the $j$-th **Riesz
transform** $R_j$ by its Fourier multiplier

$$m_j(\xi):=\begin{cases}-i\,\xi_j/|\xi|,&\xi\ne0,\\0,&\xi=0,\end{cases}\qquad \widehat{R_jf}=m_j\,\widehat f ,$$

where the Fourier transform is the unitary Plancherel extension $\mathcal F_2$
of [[thm-plancherel]] and the multiplier acts by
$R_j=\mathcal F_2^{-1}M_{m_j}\mathcal F_2$. The symbol $m_j$ is measurable and
$|m_j(\xi)|\le1$ for every $\xi$ on account of $|\xi_j|\le|\xi|$, so the
published $L^2$ multiplier theorem
[[lem-ltwo-fourier-multiplier-bound]] applies with essential supremum at most
one: $R_j$ is a well-defined bounded complex-linear operator on
$L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, it depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $m_j$,
and in particular the assigned value $m_j(0)=0$ has no effect on the operator.
The theorem also identifies $R_j$ on Schwartz functions with the regular
distribution of $\mathcal F_2^{-1}(m_j\mathcal F_2f)$, and gives $\|R_j\|\le1$.

The **Riesz kernel** attached to this definition is the function on
$\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$

$$K_j(x):=c_n\,\frac{x_j}{|x|^{n+1}},\qquad c_n:=\frac{\Gamma\bigl((n+1)/2\bigr)}{\pi^{(n+1)/2}} ,$$

with [[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral|$\Gamma$]] the Euler
integral. Since $(n+1)/2>0$, the published convergence theorem
[[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]] gives $0<\Gamma((n+1)/2)<\infty$,
so $c_n$ is a positive finite constant and $K_j$ is a smooth function on
$\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, odd under $x\mapsto-x$ and homogeneous of degree
$-n$: $K_j(tx)=t^{-n}K_j(x)$ for $t>0$.

This definition asserts only the multiplier description. It does not assert
that the principal value $\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{|y|>\varepsilon}
K_j(y)f(x-y)\,dy$ exists for any particular $f$ or $x$; that statement is
proved separately for Schwartz functions, as is the identification of the limit
with the $L^2$ class $R_jf$. In dimension $n=1$ the constant collapses to
$c_1=\Gamma(1)/\pi=1/\pi$, by the value $\Gamma(1)=1$ of
[[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]], and $K_1(x)=1/(\pi x)$ is the
line Hilbert kernel; the comparison of $R_1$ with the Hilbert transform of the
line is worked out on the examples page. The Fourier convention is the
$e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}$ convention of $\mathcal F_2$. Replacing its phase by
$e^{-ix\cdot\xi}$ leaves both $m_j$ and $c_n$ unchanged: the frequency
rescaling $\xi\mapsto\xi/(2\pi)$ preserves $\xi_j/|\xi|$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$ and $1\le j\le n$. The $j$-th Riesz
transform $R_j$ of [[def-riesz-transforms-on-euclidean-space]] extends uniquely
to a bounded operator on $L^p(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for every
$1<p<\infty$, with norm at most $C_{n,p}$, a constant depending only on $n$
and $p$: the Riesz kernel $K_j(x)=c_nx_j/|x|^{n+1}$ is a standard $1$-Hölder
Calderón–Zygmund kernel with constant $C_n=c_n2^{n+1}(3n+4)$, so that
$$\|R_jf\|_p\le C_{n,p}\bigl(1+|S^{n-1}|2^{-1}C_n\bigr) \max\bigl(p,(p-1)^{-1}\bigr)\|f\|_p \qquad(f\in L^p(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)).$$

Assume Countable Choice.  For $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every
multi-index $\alpha$,

$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha u) =(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu, \qquad \mathcal F(x^\alpha u) =\left(-\frac1{2\pi i}\right)^{|\alpha|} \partial_\xi^\alpha\mathcal Fu.$$

Assume Countable Choice and use the negative-sign $2\pi$ normalization.  If
$f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\widehat f},$$

where $\widehat f$ is the integral Fourier transform.  If
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, then

$$\mathcal F u_f=u_{\mathcal F_2f},$$

where $\mathcal F_2$ is the Plancherel extension.  These equalities are in

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the intersection
$$C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
is dense in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is a function
$v\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\|v-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ and no
extension of $u$ beyond $\Omega$ is assumed. The exponent $p=\infty$ is
excluded, as the companion remark records.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\eta\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. For
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, suppose that for every $\gamma\le\alpha$ there is
$v_\gamma\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$D^\gamma u=v_\gamma$ weakly. Then $\eta u$ has a weak $\alpha$-derivative,
and its almost-everywhere class is
$$D^\alpha(\eta u)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}\binom{\alpha}{\beta}(D^\beta\eta)D^{\alpha-\beta}u\quad\text{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
where $D^\beta\eta$ is the classical derivative and products are pointwise
products of representatives. The resulting class does not depend on the
representatives.

For $k\in\mathbb N_0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, if
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $D^\beta\eta\in L^\infty(\Omega)$ for
every $|\beta|\le k$, then $\eta u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and the same
formula holds in $L^p$ for every $|\alpha|\le k$. In particular,
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is a sufficient condition on the
multiplier for this global conclusion.

For $\Omega=\varnothing$ all classes are zero and the identity holds. The
pairing convention is bilinear, with no complex conjugation.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain
([[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]) and let
$1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is compactly embedded in
$L^p(\Omega)$: every sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ has a subsequence
converging in $L^p(\Omega)$. Every bounded $C^1$ domain is an example.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a

prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain with a bounded extension operator $E$, and let $1\le p<n$, $p\le q\le p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously:
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice (and hence Countable Choice and Dependent Choice). Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<n$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded connected $W^{1,p}$-extension domain. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

derivations.claim: **The whole-space first-order estimate.** For a compactly supported smooth one-form $b$ on $\mathbb R^4$ put $f_{ij}=\partial_i b_j-\partial_j b_i$ for all ordered indices and $g=\sum_i\partial_i b_i$. The identity $\Delta b_j=\sum_i\partial_i f_{ij}+\partial_j g$ and [F1] give $\partial_k b_j=-\sum_iR_kR_if_{ij}-R_kR_jg$: multiplication of the Fourier symbols proves equality away from zero frequency, hence almost everywhere in the $L^2$ transforms, and Plancherel injectivity identifies the functions. Riesz boundedness now gives $\|\nabla b\|_p\le C_{p,V}(\|db\|_p+\|d^*b\|_p)$. Approximate compactly supported $W^{1,p}$ forms by compactly supported smooth ones using [F2]; all displayed first derivatives converge in $L^p$, so the estimate extends to them.

**Reflection of a tangential one-form.** For smooth $a$ on $\overline B_1$ with $a(
u)=0$, put $\iota(x)=x/|x|^2$ on $1<|x|<2$ and $b=\iota^*a=D\iota^T a(\iota x)$ there, and put $b=a$ inside $B_1$. On the sphere $D\iota=I-2
u\otimes
u$, so the boundary values match. This continuous piecewise smooth form has its piecewise first derivatives as weak derivatives, by cancelling the value-jump terms in integration by parts. Outside the sphere, differentiating and cancelling the symmetric second derivatives of $\iota$ gives $db=\iota^*(da)$. Also $D\iota D\iota^T=|x|^{-4}I$ and $\Delta\iota_j=-4|x|^{-4}x_j$, whence $\operatorname{div}b=|x|^{-4}(\operatorname{div}a)(\iota x)+4|x|^{-2}x\cdot b$. The inversion Jacobian is $|x|^{-8}$; these formulas on the bounded annulus show that its $b,db,d^*b$ norms are controlled by the respective inside $a,da,d^*a$ norms, with an additional $C\|a\|_p$ in the codifferential estimate.

**The estimate with a compact lower-order term.** Multiply the reflected form by a fixed cutoff equal to one near $\overline B_1$ and supported in $B_2$. Its exterior derivative and codifferential acquire only bounded smooth multiples of $b$. Apply step 1.1 to the resulting compactly supported $W^{1,p}$ form and restrict to $B_1$, using step 1.2 and the product rule. This yields $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p+\|a\|_p)$. It extends to $Y_p$ by its defining strong approximation. For the same approximants, integration by parts and zero normal value give $\int\langle a_j,d\phi\rangle=\int\langle d^*a_j,\phi\rangle$; passing to the limit proves the claimed identity for $a\in Y_p$.

**The kernel has no nonzero elements.** Suppose $a\in Y_p$ has $da=d^*a=0$. The identity used in step 1.1 makes each component of $a$ distributionally harmonic, hence smooth in the ball by [F4]. Closedness gives a smooth $V$-valued potential $u(x)=\int_0^1\sum_i x_i a_i(tx)\,dt$: differentiating under the integral and using $\partial_j a_i=\partial_i a_j$ makes $\partial_j u$ the integral of $\frac{d}{dt}(t a_j(tx))$, so $du=a$. Normalize $u$ to have zero mean on $B_{1/2}$. For $1/2<R<1$, Poincare on $B_R$ gives $\|u-u_{B_R}\|_{L^2(B_R)}\le PR\|a\|_2$. Taking the mean over $B_{1/2}$ bounds $|u_{B_R}|\le |B_{1/2}|^{-1/2}P\|a\|_2$. Consequently $\|u\|_{L^2(B_R)}\le C\|a\|_2$, uniformly in $R$. Here $a\in L^2$ since $p\ge2$ and the ball has finite volume. Monotone convergence [F5] gives $u\in W^{1,2}(B_1)$ with $du=a$. The zero-normal identity of step 2.1 extends to every $W^{1,2}$ scalar test by [F5], since $a\in L^2$ and $d^*a=0$. Test with $u$ to obtain $\|a\|_2^2=0$. Thus $a=0$.

**Removing the lower-order term.** If no constant bounded the $W^{1,p}$ norm by $\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p$ on $Y_p$, choose $a_j\in Y_p$ with $\|a_j\|_{W^{1,p}}=1$ and $\|da_j\|_p+\|d^*a_j\|_p<1/j$. By [F3] a subsequence converges in $L^p$. Apply step 2.1 to its pairwise differences; their first-order data tend to zero, so the subsequence is Cauchy in $W^{1,p}$. Completeness follows componentwise from [F5] by passing the derivative test identities to the $L^p$ limits. The strong limit $a\in Y_p$ therefore has norm one, but $da=d^*a=0$, contrary to step 3.1. This proves $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p)$ on the unit ball.

**Critical nonlinear absorption.** For $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$, the Frobenius matrix inequality gives $|[X,Y]|\le2|X||Y|$ and hence $|a\wedge a|\le2|a|^2$. Fix $2\le p<4$ and let $p^*=4p/(4-p)$. By [F3] there is $S_p$ with $\|a\|_{p^*}\le S_p\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}$. For $d^*a=0$, step 4.1 and Holder give $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C_{p,V}(\|F_a\|_p+2\|a\|_4\|a\|_{p^*})$, since $1/p=1/4+1/p^*$. Choose $\rho_p=(4C_{p,V}S_p)^{-1}$. Then $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$ absorbs the last term and gives $\|a\|_{W^{1,p}}\le2C_{p,V}\|F_a\|_p$. All curvature products are in $L^p$, since $p^*\ge2p$ for $p\ge2$ on a finite-volume ball.

**All radii and conclusion.** Pull back by $y\mapsto ry$, so $b(y)=r a(ry)$. Smooth zero-normal forms pull back to smooth zero-normal forms, and strong approximation shows that $Y_p$ pulls back to $Y_p$. The $L^p$ norms of $\nabla b,db,d^*b$ scale by $r^{2-4/p}$, while $\|b\|_p=r^{1-4/p}\|a\|_p$. Also $F_b(y)=r^2F_a(ry)$ and $\|b\|_4=\|a\|_4$. Dividing the unit-ball estimates of steps 4.1–5.1 by $r^{2-4/p}$ proves both stated bounds. The integration identity rescales directly, and the kernel assertion follows from the estimate. Full AC is used through the exact Fourier, compactness and approximation suppliers [F1]–[F6], including the sequential choices in step 4.1.

Assume full AC. Derivative tensors carry their Euclidean norms, and Sobolev norms are sums of the resulting $L^p$ norms. Fix a finite-dimensional real inner-product space $V$, $2\le p<\infty$, and $r>0$. Every $f\in L^p(B_r(0);V)$ with zero volume mean has a unique mean-zero $u\in W^{2,p}(B_r;V)$ satisfying
$$\int_{B_r}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{B_r}\langle f,v\rangle\qquad(v\in W^{1,2}(B_r;V)).$$
The inverse is linear and obeys
$$r^{-2}\|u\|_p+r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_p+\|D^2u\|_p\le C_{p,V}\|f\|_p,$$
with $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ and $f$. Its solution is the $W^{2,p}$ limit of mean-zero polynomial solutions with classical zero normal derivative. In particular it belongs to the $W^{2,p}$ closure of smooth zero-normal-derivative functions on the closed ball.

On $B_1$, let $X_p$ be the $W^{2,p}$ closure of the $V$-valued polynomials with zero normal derivative on the sphere, and let $X_p^0$ be its mean-zero subspace. Then $-\Delta:X_p^0\to L^p_0(B_1;V)$ is a bounded bijection with the above inverse. Here $L^p_0$ denotes the zero-mean subspace; $X_p^0$ is complete for the equivalent norm $\|u\|_{X_p^0}=\|\Delta u\|_p$. A prescribed finite orthogonal equivariance of $f$ is preserved by the inverse, as in the $L^2$ case. No endpoint $p=\infty$ or nonlinear gauge existence is asserted.

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a fixed finite-dimensional real inner-product space, $2\le p<\infty$, and $B_r=B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$. Let $Y_p(B_r;V)$ be the $W^{1,p}$ closure of smooth $V$-valued one-forms on the closed ball satisfying $a(\nu)=0$ on the sphere. Write $d^*a=-\sum_i\partial_i a_i$ and $(da)_{ij}=\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i$ for $i<j$. There is $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ such that every $a\in Y_p(B_r;V)$ satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_{p,V}\bigl(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p\bigr).$$
Every such $a$ satisfies the zero-normal integration identity $\int\langle a,d\phi\rangle=\int\langle d^*a,\phi\rangle$ for smooth $\phi$ on the closed ball. If $da=d^*a=0$, then $a=0$.

For $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with the Frobenius norm and $2\le p<4$, there exist $\rho_p>0$ and $C_p$ independent of $r$ such that, whenever $a\in Y_p$ satisfies $d^*a=0$ and $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$, its curvature $F_a=da+a\wedge a$, $(a\wedge a)_{ij}=[a_i,a_j]$, satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_p\|F_a\|_p.$$

derivations.claim: **Sobolev matrix algebra and boundary approximation.** By [F3]–[F4] and the weak product rule obtained by smooth approximation, $\|vw\|_{W^{2,3}}\le K_A\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}\|w\|_{W^{2,3}}$: the second-derivative cross terms obey $\|DvDw\|_3\le\|Dv\|_6\|Dw\|_6$, and [F3] controls both $L^6$ norms. Similarly $\|cv\|_{W^{1,3}}+\|vc\|_{W^{1,3}}\le K_A\|c\|_{W^{1,3}}\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Passing the derivative test identities to $L^3$ limits proves completeness of the ambient Sobolev spaces from [F4]. The power series for $e^u$ therefore converges in $W^{2,3}$, locally uniformly in that norm, and defines a continuously differentiable composition there; termwise differentiation is justified by the convergent exponential majorants. For $u\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ pointwise, $u^2=-s^2I$ for a real $s$, so $e^u=\cos s\,I+(\sin s/s)u$ (with the continuous value at zero) is unitary with determinant one. Polynomial Neumann approximants to $u\in X$ exponentiate to smooth $SU(2)$ maps with zero normal derivative; continuity gives $e^u\in\mathcal G_N$. Products of maps in $\mathcal G_N$ remain in it, and inverse is matrix adjoint and hence continuous. Gauge transformation by such maps sends $Y$ to $Y$, by approximating both inputs with smooth zero-normal inputs and using the above product estimates. Also $du\in Y$ for $u\in X$.

**The exact nonlinear remainder.** Put $h=e^u$ and define $R(u)=h^{-1}dh-du+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h-a$. By step 1.1, $R(u)\in Y$ whenever $u\in X$. Let $E(u)=e^{-u}d(e^u)-du$. Differentiating the convergent matrix series, or integrating the series termwise, gives $e^{-u}d(e^u)=\int_0^1e^{-tu}(du)e^{tu}\,dt$, hence $E(u)=A(u)du$ where $A(0)=0$ and $A$ and its first two matrix derivatives are uniformly bounded for $|u|\le1$. More precisely $|A(u)|\le C|u|$ there. Thus $R(u)=E(u)+(e^{-u}ae^u-a)+e^{-u}\lambda e^u$, with $R(0)=\lambda$.

**The quadratic differential term.** Suppose $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}},\|v\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta$ with $\eta$ small enough that [F3] gives $|u|,|v|\le1$. The formula in step 2.1 gives $|d^*E(u)|\le C(|u||D^2u|+|Du|^2)$. Subtracting the two formulas, using bounded first and second derivatives of $A$, and applying [F3]–[F4] gives $\|d^*E(u)\|_3\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}^2$ and $\|d^*(E(u)-E(v))\|_3\le C\eta\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Indeed terms with two first derivatives use $L^6\cdot L^6\subset L^3$, while a second derivative is paired with an $L^\infty$ factor; differences of coefficients are bounded by $C|u-v|$, and the resulting terms use the same two estimates. These formulas hold for the Sobolev classes by the smooth approximation and product continuity of step 1.1.

**The critical Coulomb coefficient and the perturbation.** In $d^*(e^{-u}ae^u-a)$ the term $e^{-u}(d^*a)e^u-d^*a$ vanishes. Only derivatives falling on the exponentials remain, so their pointwise norm is at most $C|a||Du|$ for $|u|\le1$. Subtracting at $u,v$ gives at most $C|a|(|D(u-v)|+|u-v|(|Du|+|Dv|))$. By $L^4\cdot L^{12}\subset L^3$, this gives a difference bound $C\|a\|_4\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$ when $\eta\le1$. The contracted derivative of $e^{-u}\lambda e^u$ consists of $e^{-u}(d^*\lambda)e^u$ and terms bounded by $C|\lambda||Du|$. The same subtraction, [F3] and Holder give a difference bound $C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. Thus, after choosing one universal $C_0$, steps 3.1–4.1 prove $\|d^*(R(u)-R(v))\|_3\le C_0(\eta+\|a\|_4+\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}})\|u-v\|_{W^{2,3}}$. The cancellation of $d^*a$ is why no higher norm of $a$ occurs in this bound.

**A well-defined contraction, including compatibility.** Define $T(u)=S(-d^*R(u))$ on the closed radius-$\eta$ ball in $X$. Step 2.1 and [F2] show $-d^*R(u)\in L^3_0$, so the Neumann solve is well defined for every iterate. Choose positive $\eta,\rho$ so that $\eta\le1$, the $L^\infty$ restriction of step 3.1 holds, and $K_NC_0(\eta+\rho)\le1/4$. Then choose $\delta>0$ so small that $K_NC_0\delta\le1/4$ and $K_N\|d^*\lambda\|_3\le\eta/4$ whenever $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le\delta$; the latter follows from the fixed finite coefficient bound for $d^*$. For $\|a\|_4\le\rho$ and such $\lambda$, step 4.1 gives contraction constant at most $1/2$, and $\|T(0)\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta/4$. Hence $\|T(u)\|_{W^{2,3}}\le3\eta/4$ on that ball. It is a complete metric space by [F1] and the equivalence of its domain norm with $W^{2,3}$.

**The correction and uniqueness.** By [F4], $u_{j+1}=T(u_j)$ starting at zero converges to the unique fixed point $u$ in that ball. The equation $-\Delta u=-d^*R(u)$ and $d^*du=-\Delta u$ give $d^*(du+R(u))=0$. Since $d^*a=0$, the form $b=a+du+R(u)=h^{-1}dh+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h$ is Coulomb and belongs to $Y$ by step 1.1. Conversely any $u\in X$ in the stated ball for which $b$ is Coulomb satisfies this same Neumann equation, so uniqueness of [F1] makes it a fixed point and thus this $u$. Also $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\|T(0)\|_{W^{2,3}}+\tfrac12\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le K_N\|d^*\lambda\|_3+\tfrac12\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, giving the first quantitative bound.

**The correction size in the connection norm.** The matrix power series and product estimates of step 1.1 imply $\|e^{-u}d(e^u)\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, $\|e^{-u}ae^u-a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}$, and $\|e^{-u}\lambda e^u\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}$ on the fixed small ball. For the middle bound, write $e^{-u}ae^u-a=(e^{-u}-1)ae^u+a(e^u-1)$; the terms with derivatives on $a$ have a factor bounded by $C\|u\|_\infty$, and the other terms use $L^4\cdot L^{12}\subset L^3$. Adding the three bounds and using step 6.1 proves the claimed estimate for $b-a$, with $C$ independent of $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}$.

**Prescribed finite equivariance.** Orthogonal pullback preserves the Laplacian, codifferential, means and all the domain norms. Constant unitary conjugation preserves matrix products, the Frobenius norm and the exponential. Therefore the transformation $u(x)\mapsto d\tau_\gamma^{-1}(u(\gamma x))$ preserves $X$ and commutes with $T$ when $a,\lambda$ have the stated equivariance; this uses the equivariant inverse of [F1]. The zero starting iterate is invariant, so every iterate and its limit are invariant. Exponentiation gives the assertion for $h$. A central unitary scalar acts trivially by conjugation, which explains why a $PU(2)$ action suffices. The existence, uniqueness, estimates and boundary compatibility are all supplied in steps 5.1–7.1; full AC is inherited as stated in [F5].

Assume full AC. Let $V$ be a fixed finite-dimensional real inner-product space, $2\le p<\infty$, and $B_r=B_r(0)\subset\mathbb R^4$. Let $Y_p(B_r;V)$ be the $W^{1,p}$ closure of smooth $V$-valued one-forms on the closed ball satisfying $a(\nu)=0$ on the sphere. Write $d^*a=-\sum_i\partial_i a_i$ and $(da)_{ij}=\partial_i a_j-\partial_j a_i$ for $i<j$. There is $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ such that every $a\in Y_p(B_r;V)$ satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_{p,V}\bigl(\|da\|_p+\|d^*a\|_p\bigr).$$
Every such $a$ satisfies the zero-normal integration identity $\int\langle a,d\phi\rangle=\int\langle d^*a,\phi\rangle$ for smooth $\phi$ on the closed ball. If $da=d^*a=0$, then $a=0$.

For $V=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with the Frobenius norm and $2\le p<4$, there exist $\rho_p>0$ and $C_p$ independent of $r$ such that, whenever $a\in Y_p$ satisfies $d^*a=0$ and $\|a\|_4\le\rho_p$, its curvature $F_a=da+a\wedge a$, $(a\wedge a)_{ij}=[a_i,a_j]$, satisfies
$$r^{-1}\|a\|_p+\|\nabla a\|_p\le C_p\|F_a\|_p.$$
All norms here are Euclidean coefficient norms; the class $Y_p$ states precisely the boundary approximation hypothesis.

Assume full AC and work on the closed Euclidean unit ball in four dimensions. Use sums of $L^p$ norms of Euclidean ordered derivative tensors for Sobolev norms; these are equivalent to the cited scalar Sobolev norms and invariant under orthogonal coordinate changes. Let $X$ be the mean-zero $W^{2,3}$ closure of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued polynomials with zero normal derivative on the sphere. Let $Y$ be the $W^{1,3}$ closure of smooth $\mathfrak{su}(2)$-valued one-forms with zero normal component on the sphere. Let $\mathcal G_N$ be the $W^{2,3}$ closure of smooth maps to $SU(2)$ with zero normal derivative on the sphere.

There exist fixed positive constants $\rho,\eta,\delta,C$ such that, if $a\in Y$ satisfies $d^*a=0$, $\|a\|_4\le\rho$, and $\lambda\in Y$ satisfies $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le\delta$, there exists $u\in X$, unique among $\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le\eta$, such that $h=e^u\in\mathcal G_N$ and
$$b=h^{-1}dh+h^{-1}(a+\lambda)h\in Y,\qquad d^*b=0.$$
Moreover
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,3}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}},\qquad \|b-a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C(1+\|a\|_{W^{1,3}})\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}.$$
All constants are independent of the higher norm of $a$.

Given a finite $\Gamma\le O(4)$ and an action $\tau$ of $\Gamma$ on $SU(2)$ by constant unitary conjugations, suppose $\gamma^*a=d\tau_\gamma(a)$ and $\gamma^*\lambda=d\tau_\gamma(\lambda)$. Then $u(\gamma x)=d\tau_\gamma(u(x))$ and $h(\gamma x)=\tau_\gamma(h(x))$. A representation into $PU(2)$ supplies such a conjugation action; no lift of that representation to $SU(2)$ is required.

Assume full AC. Derivative tensors carry their Euclidean norms, and Sobolev norms are sums of the resulting $L^p$ norms. Fix a finite-dimensional real inner-product space $V$, $2\le p<\infty$, and $r>0$. Every $f\in L^p(B_r(0);V)$ with zero volume mean has a unique mean-zero $u\in W^{2,p}(B_r;V)$ satisfying
$$\int_{B_r}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{B_r}\langle f,v\rangle\qquad(v\in W^{1,2}(B_r;V)).$$
The inverse is linear and obeys
$$r^{-2}\|u\|_p+r^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_p+\|D^2u\|_p\le C_{p,V}\|f\|_p,$$
with $C_{p,V}$ independent of $r$ and $f$. Its solution is the $W^{2,p}$ limit of mean-zero polynomial solutions with classical zero normal derivative. In particular it belongs to the $W^{2,p}$ closure of smooth zero-normal-derivative functions on the closed ball.

On $B_1$, let $X_p$ be the $W^{2,p}$ closure of the $V$-valued polynomials with zero normal derivative on the sphere, and let $X_p^0$ be its mean-zero subspace. Then $-\Delta:X_p^0\to L^p_0(B_1;V)$ is a bounded bijection with the above inverse. Here $L^p_0$ denotes the zero-mean subspace; $X_p^0$ is complete for the equivalent norm $\|u\|_{X_p^0}=\|\Delta u\|_p$. A prescribed finite orthogonal equivariance of $f$ is preserved by the inverse, as in the $L^2$ case. No endpoint $p=\infty$ or nonlinear gauge existence is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $W^{1,p}$-extension domain with a bounded extension operator $E$, and let $1\le p<n$, $p\le q\le p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. Then $W^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$ continuously:
$$\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(n,p,q,\Omega)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the intersection
$$C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)\cap W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
is dense in $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is a function
$v\in C^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $v\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\|v-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ and no
extension of $u$ beyond $\Omega$ is assumed. The exponent $p=\infty$ is
excluded, as the companion remark records.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: **A constructed radial gauge.** Put $M(s,x)=\sum_i x_iA_i(sx)$ and define $P(s,x)$ by the convergent iterated-integral series $I+\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^k\int_{0<t_k<\cdots<t_1<s}M(t_1,x)\cdots M(t_k,x)\,dt_k\cdots dt_1$. On the compact parameter set every term has norm at most $L^k/k!$; any fixed number $N$ of spatial derivatives is bounded by $C_N k^N L_N^k/k!$. Uniform convergence of these derivative series, followed by the coordinate-segment fundamental theorem, identifies them as the derivatives of the sum. The series also gives the integral equation $P(s,x)=I-\int_0^sM(t,x)P(t,x)\,dt$, which also gives smoothness in $s$. It satisfies $\partial_sP=-MP$, $P(0,x)=I$. Since $M$ is skew-Hermitian and trace zero, differentiation gives $\partial_s(P^*P)=0$; thus $P$ is unitary, and the two-by-two determinant derivative gives $\partial_s\det P=-\operatorname{tr}(M)\det P=0$, so $P\in SU(2)$. Uniqueness of the integral equation follows by iterating its difference estimate $k$ times and taking $k\to\infty$ using $L^k/k!\to0$. Set $U(x)=P(1,x)$. Rescaling the integration parameters gives $U(sx)=P(s,x)$, so $x\cdot dU=-(x\cdot A)U$. Therefore $C=A^U$ is smooth and $x\cdot C=0$.

**Gauge algebra and the scaling path.** The matrix identity $d(g^{-1})=-g^{-1}(dg)g^{-1}$ gives $F_{A^g}=g^{-1}F_Ag$ and $(A^g)^h=A^{gh}$ by expansion and cancellation. It applies to smooth gauges first; [F4]–[F5] pass it to $W^{2,3}$ gauges and their $W^{1,3}$ connection forms. Unitarity preserves pointwise curvature norms. Define $A_t(x)=tC(tx)$ for $0\le t\le1$. It is a smooth path of smooth zero-normal forms, starts at zero, and ends at $C$. Its curvature is $F_{A_t}(x)=t^2F_C(tx)$, hence $\|F_{A_t}\|_2=\|F_C\|_{L^2(B_t)}\le\|F_A\|_2$ for $t>0$, and $\|F_{A_t}\|_3=t^{2/3}\|F_C\|_{L^3(B_t)}\le\|F_C\|_3$. The same inequalities at $t=0$ are immediate. There are finite constants $L,X$ for which $\|A_t-A_s\|_{W^{1,3}}\le L|t-s|$ and $1+\sup_t(\|A_t\|_{W^{1,3}}+\|F_{A_t}\|_3)\le X$: differentiate $tC(tx)$ and $t^2DC(tx)$ in $t$, using bounded derivatives of the fixed smooth $C$ through order two.

**Uniform critical improvement in any admissible gauge.** Choose $\rho>0$ no larger than $\rho_c,\rho_2,\rho_3$ in [F1]–[F2]. Call $t$ admissible if some $g\in\mathcal G_N$ has $a=A_t^g\in Y_3$, $d^*a=0$ and $\|a\|_4\le\rho$. All such forms belong to $Y_2$ by finite-volume norm comparison of their smooth normal approximants. By [F1], curvature covariance and [F4], there is a fixed $K_0$ such that $\|a\|_{W^{1,2}}\le C_2\|F_A\|_2$ and $\|a\|_4\le K_0\|F_A\|_2$. Also $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_3\|F_{A_t}\|_3\le C_3X$. Choose the theorem's fixed $\varepsilon>0$ so that $K_0\varepsilon\le\rho/4$. Consequently every admissible gauge has the improved margin $\|a\|_4\le\rho/4$, and its higher connection norm is bounded by a constant depending only on $X$. These estimates require only the given curvature bound, once admissibility holds.

**A uniform bound on the transported perturbation.** In an admissible gauge, $dg=g a-A_tg$ holds as a weak matrix identity. Unitarity and [F4] give $\|dg\|_{12}\le C(\|a\|_{12}+\|A_t\|_{12})\le C_X$, with $C_X$ independent of $t$ and of the chosen admissible gauge. For another parameter $s$, set $\lambda=g^{-1}(A_s-A_t)g$. Product differentiation, $g^{-1}=g^*$, Holder and $W^{1,3}\hookrightarrow L^4$ give $\|\lambda\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C(1+\|dg\|_{12})\|A_s-A_t\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_XL|s-t|$. Moreover $\lambda\in Y_3$: approximate $g$ by the defining smooth Neumann gauges of $\mathcal G_N$; conjugating the smooth zero-normal form $A_s-A_t$ by these gauges preserves zero normal component, and [F5] gives convergence in $W^{1,3}$.

**A uniform admissibility step.** Let $K_4$ be the fixed embedding norm from $W^{1,3}$ to $L^4$. Using the uniform bound for $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}$ in step 3.1, choose $\delta_X>0$ below the perturbation threshold of [F2] and so small that $K_4C_c(1+C_3X)\delta_X\le\rho/4$. Choose $\kappa>0$ so that $C_XL\kappa<\delta_X$, replacing $L$ by $1+L$ in this choice if necessary. Whenever $t$ is admissible and $|s-t|<\kappa$, step 4.1 allows [F2] to correct $a+\lambda$ by $h\in\mathcal G_N$. The result is $b=(a+\lambda)^h=A_s^{gh}\in Y_3$, Coulomb, and $\|b-a\|_4\le\rho/4$. The group $\mathcal G_N$ is closed under multiplication by the Sobolev product and approximation argument in [F2], so $gh\in\mathcal G_N$. Step 3.1 gives $\|b\|_4\le\rho/2<\rho$. Thus $s$ is admissible, with the same step length $\kappa$ for every admissible $t$.

**Finite construction reaches the original connection.** At $t=0$, take $g=I$ and $a=0$, so admissibility holds. Choose a positive integer $N$ with $1/N<\kappa$ and successively apply step 5.1 to $t_j=j/N$, $j=0,\ldots,N$. This finite induction constructs an admissible $G\in\mathcal G_N$ at $t=1$, with $a=C^G$ Coulomb and in $Y_3$. Take the total gauge $g=UG$. Step 2.1 gives $a=A^g$, and step 3.1 gives $\|a\|_{W^{1,2}}+\|a\|_4\le(C_2+K_0)\|F_A\|_2$ and $\|a\|_{W^{1,3}}\le C_3\|F_A\|_3$. In particular the construction obtains a gauge from small curvature alone. It used no assumed small potential norm of the original connection: the admissible small potentials were constructed from the zero starting connection by finitely many proved correction steps.

**Higher regularity from the constructed Neumann inverse.** The family gauge $G$ is in $W^{2,3}$ and obeys $\partial_iG=G a_i-(A_1)_iG$. Contracting its derivative and using $\sum_i\partial_i a_i=0$ gives $\Delta G=\sum_i((\partial_iG)a_i-(A_1)_i\partial_iG)-(\operatorname{div}A_1)G$. Initially $\nabla G,a\in L^{12}$ by [F4], while $A_1$ is smooth and $G$ is bounded; hence the right side belongs to $L^6$. The form $dG$ belongs to $Y_3$ with target the real eight-dimensional matrix space, by the defining smooth Neumann approximation of $G$. The integration identity of [F1] applied to $dG$ therefore gives the zero-normal weak identity for each component of $G$. In particular $-\Delta G$ has zero mean. Apply [F3] at $p=6$ to each component, after subtracting its mean, and use weak-solution uniqueness to conclude $G\in W^{2,6}$. By [F4] its first derivatives are now bounded; the displayed equation then has bounded right side, because $a=G^{-1}dG+G^{-1}A_1G$ is bounded as well. For every finite $p\ge2$, apply [F3] again to this same zero-mean source and uniqueness to obtain $G\in W^{2,p}$. The smooth factor $U$ preserves this regularity for the total gauge $g$, and the gauge formula gives $a\in W^{1,p}$ by ordinary weak product differentiation. This proves exactly the claimed Sobolev regularity, without asserting unproved smooth boundary bootstrapping.

**Given finite equivariance.** Suppose the stated $\Gamma,\tau$ data are present. The equality $M(s,\gamma x)=d\tau_\gamma(M(s,x))$ follows from the equivariance of $A$ evaluated on the radial vector. Constant conjugation commutes with all products and integrals in step 1.1, so $U(\gamma x)=\tau_\gamma(U(x))$. Hence $C$ and every $A_t$ have the same equivariance. The initial gauge $I$ is equivariant. If an admissible family gauge is equivariant, its transported perturbation in step 4.1 is equivariant, and [F2] supplies an equivariant correction. The finite induction of step 6.1 therefore produces equivariant $G$ and total $g=UG$. Only the conjugation action is used; scalar representatives of a projective unitary element act trivially, so a lift to an $SU(2)$ representation is unnecessary.

**Scaling and overlap compatibility.** For $B_r$, pull back the connection as $A_r(y)=rA(ry)$. Its critical curvature norm equals $\|F_A\|_2$. Apply the unit-ball construction and define the physical gauge by $g(x)=g_r(x/r)$. Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]], is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then

[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Then $\partial_1^2I=\mathrm{id}$, and $I$ commutes with $\Delta'=\partial_2^2+\partial_3^2+\partial_4^2$. For a polynomial $f$, choose $M$ so that $(\Delta')^{M+1}f=0$ and set $p=-\sum_{k=0}^M(-1)^kI^{k+1}(\Delta')^kf$. Applying $\partial_1^2+\Delta'$ telescopes the finite sum and gives $\Delta p=-f$.
